chunks: "At the most basic level, electricity is the movement of electric charge, and the energy that charge carries.
A source like a battery uses chemistry to create a voltage, which is just a difference in potential energy per unit charge between its terminals.
When you connect a closed loop of wire and a load, that voltage sets up an electric field along the conductor.
Metals already have tons of free electrons, so the field pushes them along. That flow of charge is current. The electrons don't move freely though.
They keep bumping into the vibrating atoms of the metal, which is resistance, so the current ends up proportional to the voltage: Ohm's law, V equals IR .
Wherever there's resistance, the energy turns into heat or light or motion, and the power is V times I . A couple of things people find surprising.
The battery doesn't supply electrons. They were already in the wire; it supplies energy to push them around the loop, which is why you need a complete circuit.
And the electrons themselves move really slowly, something like a tenth of a millimetre per second in a typical wire.
But the light turns on instantly because the field, and the energy, travel close to the speed of light."
